Name: length_prior_anchoring
Title: The Self-Fulfilling Length Prior: A Pre-Generation Budget Representation That Sets Reasoning Length Before Reasoning Begins
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models decide roughly how long to think before they think: the prompt-final hidden state (before any reasoning token is emitted) linearly encodes an expected-length / budget prior that is substantially driven by superficial prompt features (phrasing, apparent verbosity cues, presence of numbers) rather than true difficulty, and this prior causally sets trace length in a self-fulfilling way. Steering this pre-generation prior changes trace length largely independently of accuracy, revealing that a chunk of overthinking (and some underthinking) is a mis-set budget, not a reasoning need.
Related Work: Prior work reads difficulty pre-generation to *allocate* compute (Probing the Difficulty Perception Mechanism; CODA/AdaCtrl budgeting), reads early correctness/commitment signals a few tokens in (Temporal Predictors of Outcome; Chain-of-Probe), or shows the first step disproportionately shapes outcomes (Lost at the Beginning of Reasoning). All treat the model's length as an emergent consequence of the reasoning it happens to do, and treat any pre-generation signal as tracking genuine difficulty. Our phenomenon is different and, to our knowledge, untested: that a length/budget *prior* is set at the prompt boundary before a single reasoning token exists, that it is dissociable from difficulty (driven partly by superficial prompt features), and that it causally and self-fulfillingly determines trace length. This is not another difficulty-budgeting method nor an early-exit signal; it is a claim that reasoning length is anchored by a prior that can be miscalibrated and causally re-set. It also differs from my prior proposals, which all read *during* generation whether the answer is known and then stop; here the operative signal exists before generation and concerns budget, not answer-commitment.
Abstract: Reasoning language models produce chains of thought whose length varies enormously, and this length is usually assumed to reflect how much reasoning a problem actually requires. We challenge that assumption. We hypothesize that models set an approximate length budget before they begin reasoning: the hidden state at the prompt boundary, prior to emitting any reasoning token, linearly encodes an expected-length prior that is only partly tied to true difficulty and is also driven by superficial prompt features (phrasing style, verbosity cues such as 'think carefully', presence of numbers, question framing). The model then generates to fill this budget, making it self-fulfilling. We test this on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA using open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3). First, we train a linear probe on prompt-final activations to predict the eventual trace length and show it predicts length well before any reasoning occurs. Second, we dissociate the prior from difficulty: we hold the underlying problem fixed while varying only surface phrasing, and show the length prior (and realized length) shifts even though difficulty and correct answer do not, and that the probe's prediction tracks phrasing more than pass-rate. Third, we causally test self-fulfillment by steering along the length-prior direction and measuring whether trace length moves in the predicted direction while accuracy stays roughly flat, indicating mis-set budget rather than reasoning need. We localize the components carrying the prior via activation patching. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking and underthinking as an anchored, miscalibrated budget prior and offers an interpretable, training-free knob for length control.
Experiments: 1) Length-prior probing (Location): For each problem, generate a reasoning trace and record its length (reasoning-token count). Extract the prompt-final residual-stream activation (last prompt token, before any reasoning token). Train a linear probe (per layer) to predict eventual trace length (regression) from this pre-generation state. Metrics: R^2 / Spearman correlation between predicted and realized length; layer sweep to localize the signal. Baselines: predicting length from prompt token-count and from a pre-generation difficulty probe (trained on empirical pass-rate). Key claim: the pre-generation state predicts length above and beyond difficulty. 2) Difficulty dissociation (core phenomenon): Construct surface-variant prompts of the SAME problem that leave the answer and true difficulty unchanged but vary phrasing (e.g., terse vs elaborate wording, adding 'think step by step and be thorough' vs 'answer concisely', paraphrases, number-format changes). Measure (a) realized trace length, (b) probe-predicted length prior, and (c) accuracy across variants. Hypothesis: length prior and realized length shift substantially across surface variants while accuracy stays stable, and the probe tracks the surface variant more than the (constant) difficulty. Report within-problem variance in length attributable to phrasing vs difficulty via a mixed-effects model. 3) Self-fulfillment causal test (Causal Intervention): Derive a length-prior steering direction (difference-of-means between short-trace and long-trace prompt-final activations, or the probe weight vector). At the prompt boundary, add/subtract this direction (dose-response coefficient sweep) and generate. Measure change in realized trace length and accuracy. Controls: matched random direction and difficulty-direction steering (to show length moves specifically with the length-prior direction, and that accuracy is largely preserved when reducing length in the overthinking regime). Report sign, dose-response, and specificity. 4) Localization (activation patching): Patch the prompt-final activation from a short-budget prompt into a long-budget prompt (and vice versa) and measure the shift in realized length, identifying which layers/components carry the causal prior; ablate candidate components and measure length change. 5) Miscalibration and efficiency implications: Quantify how often the length prior is mis-set (long budget on easy problems -> overthinking; short budget on hard problems -> underthinking) by comparing prior-predicted length to a difficulty-matched 'needed' length (estimated via truncate-and-resume minimal solve length). Test a simple training-free correction: steer the prior toward a difficulty-appropriate target and report token-reduction-at-equal-accuracy vs no intervention, fixed truncation, and budget-forcing baselines. Metrics: accuracy, mean tokens, tokens-at-fixed-accuracy, wall-clock speedup. 6) Generalization: transfer the length-prior probe and steering direction across datasets and model scales without retraining.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The pre-generation length prior may be strongly correlated with genuine difficulty, making the dissociation hard to establish; the fixed-problem surface-variant design directly targets this, and a null dissociation would itself be an informative result (length is difficulty-driven after all). Surface-variant construction could inadvertently change difficulty; we mitigate by verifying answer/accuracy invariance and using human-checked paraphrases. Steering the prior may push activations off-distribution and degrade coherence, confounding the accuracy read; we report sample validity and use matched-direction controls. Reducing a mis-set long budget may still hurt accuracy on some items (the budget was partly needed), bounding the efficiency claim; the truncate-and-resume needed-length analysis characterizes this. Trace-length regression is noisy for short traces; we focus on tasks with substantial reasoning. Results may be model-family and scale specific, and the strength of surface-feature influence likely varies with instruction tuning.
